newsitem.title: UK: London gold sheds gains from U.S. strike on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: London gold sheds gains from U.S. strike on Iraq.

text.p: Gold gave up its minimal gains on Tuesday afternoon after ticking higher early in the morning following U.S. missile strikes on Iraq, dealers said.
Bullion fixed at $386.60 an ounce, compared with $387.20 in the morning and a London close of $386.65/$387.15.
It had hit a high bid of $387.50 shortly after news of the strikes was announced as Far Eastern buying kicked in.

But prices proceeded to drift lower during European trading. "You'd expect something more with New York coming back (after Monday's Labor Day holiday) and the Middle East news. But this is gold, not oil," a dealer said.
Prices were expected to remain in a $385-$390 trading range for the time being, with the $386 and $388 levels providing interim support and resistance, dealers said.
European and Asian dealers had been waiting for the opening of New York's Comex futures market to spark interest in gold.
But Comex December gold was indicated down $0.20 at $391.10.
Unless the conflict between the U.S. and Iraq escalated severely, gold prices were unlikely to pick up until mid-September when the seasonal lull wrapped up, dealers said.
But even an initial knee-jerk reaction higher would likely prove short-lived, dealers and analysts said.
A surge in oil prices from the tension suggested a possible surge in world inflation, which could boost gold.
But a hike in U.S. interest rates to combat the rise would diminished gold's attractiveness as an investment, they said.
"This is probably bearish. The idea that higher inflation fears is good for gold has faded after seeing gold doing nothing whenever the CRB index goes roaring up," a dealer said.
Analysts said that gold could test its 50-day moving average at $386 if it failed to reach the 200-day level at $392.00.
Oil prices came off a rally driven by the air strikes, and U.S. stocks and bonds dropped sharply.
Silver followed gold lower after an initial firming following the missile strikes.
It was indicated at $5.16/$5.18, off two cents from Monday's London close, after reaching a high bid of $5.21 an ounce early in the day.
Dealers expected silver to remain in a $5.15-$5.25 range for the time being.
Platinum was up just five cents at $395.55/$396.55, while palladium was just 10 cents lower at $125.40/$126.40.
